utterances.text: That is normally 500 to 600 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a HVO battalion, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less because it was difficult -- some of the brigades down there had only 100 men, and some of them have 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you have already asked this question, Mr. Hayman. There have been very many questions about the military organisation of the HVO et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say you believe the operation on 16th April was planned at a high level, what level do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Higher than brigade level, because, as I told you just before, some of the brigades were only having maybe 100 or 300 people, so therefore it should be more than a brigade commander to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your judgment that it involved however many brigades were necessary to add up to at least 500 men; is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your opinion is, put another way, that any combination of men that would reach 500 could have been the level at which it was planned, as long as it was co-ordination between those units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To plan the type of operation that you observed on 16th April, I would like to try and form a mental list with you; I want you to articulate it for us, of what would have to be done. Let me ask you some questions in that regard. In your opinion, would stockpiles of ammunitions have to be predeployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Predeployed or taken with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not believe munitions would have to be prestaged or prelocated somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they were not, would they have to be gathered at a munitions depot or warehouse and issued to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because if they were going to deploy all the ammunition before the attack, then the other part would know that something was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So either munitions had to be predeployed or the soldiers had to be rounded up somewhere approximate to a munitions facility or warehouse and issued extra munitions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would any battlefield communications equipment have to be predeployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally you are bringing your radios with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just take them with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks would it take to transport 500 to 600 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends on the need, the transport, because normally the infantry are using their feet, and the distance from Vitez to Ahmici is not longer than soldiers are able to walk by foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying either the 600 soldiers marched to the operation; if not, how many trucks would be required to move a specific number of men? Can you fit 20 men in a truck, 40 men, 50 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would all depend on the kind of truck. I think you would have to use 30 or 40 trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you need any extra fuel? Would that have to be predeployed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would bring it with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put it in the back of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or if you go back to get some more soldiers you would have the opportunity to refuel your vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there be an operation or an exercise with respect to fighting in built-up areas before this type of well-planned operation in a built-up area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That should be the normal way to do it, because before an operation like this, you have to prepare soldiers for it. You have to tell them -- that is the normal way to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The normal way to do it is tell every soldier exactly what their task is; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and train them for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then train them to carry out that task; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To do that, would you have to gather these 500 or 600 men together for briefings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It is efficient if you just bring in the commanders and give the orders to the commanders and then the lower commanders can exercise their own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the 500 or 600 men were not gathered together in one place, is it your opinion that the specific instructions to the men in the field were issued at the brigade commander or lower levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the brigade commanders gave the orders as they have got their orders from the HVO headquarters, so the brigade commanders were the men who were responsible to train the soldiers for the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, how do you know whether the brigade commanders repeated orders or changed orders? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know whether the brigade commanders repeated orders or changed orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normal in a brigade commanders are doing what they are told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a normal army they would repeat the orders they received and the soldiers below them would obey those orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have already seen from the order we looked at about Red Cross access that there were orders given to this army that were not obeyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But the operation was carried out, was it not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A tragedy occurred, Major. Would special battle orders have to be prepared, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would those look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally in the western armies, when you are giving a battle order, you have to tell them about the task; you have to tell about your own situation, about the enemy's situation; you have to tell them how you will co-ordinate the operation; you will tell them about communications; you will tell them about logistics. That is the normal contents of a combat order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If such special combat orders are not issued, what is likely to result, if you send men out on a mission without having given those types of orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They will not be able to fulfil their operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or an uncontrolled operation will go forward; is that correct? If they are not given specific combat orders in the different areas you have identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think the soldiers, if they did not receive an order, that they would do a thing like this. Even soldiers are human beings. We saw examples down there that some individuals did things like that, but not units like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was on a larger scale, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was happening in Ahmici was not made by individuals or one group of men who did not receive an order and wanted to have something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was some number of men acting in concert in Ahmici with absolutely no regard for human life; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men was that? How many men would have been required to destroy that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no opinion? You have given us an opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I make an objection, please? Mr. Hayman has asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, make your objection, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman has asked over and over and over again the number of men involved in this operation. I think the witness has answered the question more than once and I think that this line of questioning should move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained, Mr. Hayman, you have put this question on a number of occasions. At times, you are asking the witness his opinion as a military expert whether this or that is necessary for an attack, for reserve forces et cetera, and then you tell him you do not have proof of what you are saying, so please choose your angle of approach to the matter. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have said that 500 to 600 men participated in the operation. How many of them were required in Ahmici? How many of them were required to be present in Ahmici for this operation, in your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an expert, I have never commanded a unit who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, go on to another question. Whether the expert can tell you that Ahmici was totally destroyed by so many men, that is not a pertinent question. Please do not repeat the question. Continue, I should like to remind you that you said you would finish your cross-examination this afternoon. I wish to remind you that the judges may also have certain questions to put, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand your Honour and I am moving forward with the greatest speed that I can, but I would like to note for the record that when an expert gives a number of men in an opinion that they believe were involved, the Defence should be entitled to break that number down in terms of its component parts. That was what I was trying to do. If the court insists, I will abandon that area and move on. On 14th or 15th April, what preparations for this operation did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not observe the preparations because at those two days, I was travelling in Travnik, in the Novi Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th you visited the 7th Muslim Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is some distance from Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got into Zenica at 3.00 am on the 15th, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 15th, you were back in Novi Travnik investigating the four officers who had been abducted; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not in a position to observe any preparations for this operation, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, of the 500 to 600 men you have described, what component parts would be required for that number; that is how many would participate in an infantry attack and where; how many would participate in artillery attacks, how many would man checkpoints? Can you break that number down for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends on how many artillery units you are going to man, because you have to use people to man the artillery pieces; you have to, as I said, have people to seal the whole area using the checkpoints, then you have a unit to carry out the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that you have to use half of them to carry out the attack and to help those with the logistics and the other half to man the artillery positions and the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your opinion, 250 to 300 men would be required to man the artillery and the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 250 to 300 to actually carry out infantry attacks in the Vitez and Ahmici areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and secure the movements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secure whose movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those units' own movements, because normally when you are in war and you are moving a unit, one unit would secure the move of the other unit, and when this first unit are in a prime target or area positions, then they will be guarding the area and then take the other unit in front, so I do not say that 300 men were used for the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, I think I understand the concept you are illustrating. Generally, does an artillery attack precede an infantry attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally during this artillery attack the infantry will move on and when the artillery attack stops, the infantry will attack the rest of the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will move into the target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you estimate from the tracer fire that you saw on the evening of the 16th how many men would be required to generate the amount of tracer fire you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not able to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you observe the tracer fire? A minute, ten minutes, an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we were at the road for half an hour and we saw tracer fire in that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said in your testimony that the HVO was well organised, and you drew our attention to the list of brigades which you obtained from the HVO. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "well organised", do you mean they were well organised on paper or do you mean that they functioned as an organised effective disciplined army? What did you mean when you used the term "well organised"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were well organised on paper and we saw that many of the units were organised as well, but normally, as I told you, in a brigade, in a normal brigade in a western country, there is more men than in those brigades, because some of the brigades were only manned by 100 men, some of them 300 men, so it was more like companies in a western army, but the chain of command was there, from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters to the brigade headquarters, and from the brigade headquarters to the lower levels. That was, as I say -- it was well organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand; when you say "well organised on paper" you mean they had titles for their brigades, they had soldiers broken down into brigades, they even had a telephone list which they shared with each other as well as with international organisations like ECMM; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to see that they had a headquarters at the top and this headquarters commanded a lot of subunits and those subunits commanded other subunits. This is the normal chain of command and organisation you see in all armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is being well organised on paper, would you agree; that is what that means? People are put in the right cubbyholes, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of whether the HVO functioned like a well organised effective army, that is whether there was respect for the chain of command et cetera, what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was respect for the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the HVO headquarters gave the brigade commanders orders as you showed us before, and normally those orders were carried out and the brigade commanders gave orders from this order to their units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Normally they were carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your experience with respect to orders being carried out, is that limited to authorisation to clear checkpoints or does it extend to other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other matters as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Local cease-fires in areas. I can remember we had problems in the Kakanj area where there were fightings between HVO and BiH and they were giving orders as well. They fulfilled the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, were there extraordinary problems in Central Bosnia getting cease-fire orders to stick?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the part of HVO soldiers violating cease-fires and army soldiers violating cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a large number of orders from the zone level to the brigade level were not followed, then the commander at the zone level would not have effective commanding control of the soldiers in that theatre, correct, under his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, therefore a commander -- if one of his lower commanders is not doing what he is told, he should be replaced with another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the commander has the power to do that. Normally the commander would have that power; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would and I think he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any examples of changing commanders that were fired or recalled and so forth in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember that one HVO commander in the southern part of Colonel Blaskic's area of responsibility was replaced because he refused to attack a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was during the period where there were fightings at Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this order to attack a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, probably we were told that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The locals down there; the HVO told us that this commander was replaced by another because the aforementioned commander did not want to fulfil this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Replaced by Colonel Blaskic because he refused to attack a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you told that to anyone before in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in your statement to the Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in your diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any documents or notes to support it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think and I can remember it was a matter discussed at the UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak as well, that one of the commanders in that area was replaced, and we wondered where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any notes, any documentation, any minutes, any ECMM reports to support that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can only tell the court what I heard. Maybe there will be some witness from UNPROFOR, from the headquarters in Kiseljak, who is able to tell the court about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say he was replaced because he refused to attack a civilian target, I meant he refused, as we were told, to attack a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place this, perhaps with the assistance of the usher, on the ELMO? By way of background, your Honour, this is an order from General Blaskic. The first page, front and back, is an English translation; the second page is a poor copy of a BSC original. These were provided by the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We do not have a back on ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We do not have all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, Major, before we look at the document, that if discipline becomes a critical problem in a fighting force, then those soldiers who are undisciplined must be removed from their units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their uniforms must be taken away and their weapons must be taken away; do you agree? That is the proper course of action if discipline reaches a critical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look at this order together. Perhaps we could enlarge the image and we could do it half a page at a time, please. The top, 17th March 1993, 1200 hours: "Treatment of persons inclined towards criminal and disruptive conduct. Order for the attention of...", and there is a list. For brevity I will skip over the list for now of various entities, units and so forth. If you could move the paper up slightly? "In order to prevent the recurring, openly disruptive conduct of individuals in HVO uniforms and the HVO armed formations insignia and raise combat readiness, I hereby issue the following order: "(1) immediately order platoon, company and battalion commanders at all levels to assess the conduct of conscripts and name the persons inclined toward disruptive and criminal conduct, in particular ... Responsibility: brigade commander", and there is a date given for completion and fulfilment of the order: "(2) to identify the cause, consequences of the conduct disruptive to order and discipline in an unit or command for each conscript prone to discipline conduct in the unit or command. "(3) persons prone to disruptive conduct shall return their weapons, uniform and other [rest illegible] and appropriate wartime assignment according to the decree. "(4) Should a member of an armed HVO formation decline to surrender to competent military bodies [part illegible] he shall be arrested and disarmed and disciplinary and other measures shall be obtained against him. The assistant for EMKP (abbreviation unknown) shall remove their names from the register (rest illegible). Commanders at all levels shall be responsible for covering conscripts prone to disruptive and criminal conduct, in particular who have been recorded as such in the records of platoon, company et cetera." Two more short paragraphs in terms of carrying out the order and then it indicates: "Commander: Tihomir Blaskic", signed and stamped. Would you agree that this appears to be an order designed to remove undisciplined elements from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it unusual for an order like this to have to be issued, in terms of a professional western army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen that it has been necessary in other armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have not seen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have not seen situations so extreme that this type of an order was necessary, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I want, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, is that what you are saying? Do you agree with that? I did not get an answer to the question, I am afraid. Are you saying you have not seen a situation so extreme in other armies that an order of this type was necessary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because normally other armies -- I do not know if HVO had it, we have standard operational planning, called SOP, where things like this are in, people know how to react if things like this should happen. Therefore it is not necessary to give orders like this, because this is a standing order in all other armies, that if someone are doing things like what happened there, they have to be removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in wartime, this is a difficult issue to deal with, would you agree, if discipline is breaking down at such a level that this kind of order is required? That is a difficult issue for a commander to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher could assist? I would like to ask you: you have described many burned civilian and other structures which you saw in Muslim villages or parts of villages. Would you agree that the bulk of this type of conduct, the evidence of most of this type of conduct which you observed, was on or after 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before and after. It was not an impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was wondering if your presence here was exposing us all to external forces of a different type. Before the 16th, would you agree that the burning of structures was only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is just a question of the break. Do you wish to finish with this document before the break? It is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please, your Honour. If the court wishes to break, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The hearing is adjourned until 4.15 pm. (3.55 pm) (A short break) (4.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Major, if you could place this most recent order of 22nd April on the ELMO, I would like to have just the most basic portions of the order translated by sight. If we could have the ELMO on, please? If we could zoom slightly? Thank you. It is dated 22nd April 1993 to Vares commanders. The preamble reads: "In order to prevent incidents in which houses and other commercial facilities are set on fire and looted, I hereby issue the following order: "(1) I strictly prohibit the torching of houses and other commercial facilities and looting in the zone of responsibility of the command of the Central Bosnia operations zone controlled by HVO units. "(2) Brigade and independent unit commanders must issue an order to their subordinates to make them responsible for preventing such crimes. "(3) The most stringent measures shall be taken against violators of this order pursuant to the regulation book on military discipline in HVO units." I will omit the last two paragraphs for speed: "Commander Tihomir Blaskic, signed and stamped."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us have the numbers for the exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the previous one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D42. The previous one is D42. The English version is D42A and the Croatian version D42B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that we do not have a French version for the moment. Yes, it is the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: A is the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, do you find this order extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was obviously necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could assist? I have one more order I would like to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally -- if I am allowed to speak -- when we had -- ECMM had some copies of Colonel Blaskic's orders, but we only received orders showing agreements concerning cease-fires. We never had copies of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not get a full set of either of the parties' orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is difficult for you to comment, is it not, on the internal workings and perhaps problems of the HVO? Do you think that is fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we had not seen those orders before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Believe me, I am not faulting you for material you have not seen, far from it. If you could help us, though, by placing this next exhibit on the ELMO? If the ELMO could be enlarged, the image? Thank you. The top date-line of this order is 24th April 1993, 0920 hours, titled "Prevention of Uncontrolled Conduct of Commanders and Individuals". It is addressed to commanders of all units in Central Bosnia Operative Zone and I would like to read the preamble first: "Order. After an inspection of the field, it has been observed that lower ranking commanders and their units are acting in an uncontrolled way, failing to carry out orders of their superiors, making arbitrary decisions contrary to issued orders, planning and carrying out personal combat actions, exerting pressure on civilians and interfering with the activities of UNPROFOR, ICRC and the European Monitoring Mission which has negative consequences for the HVO and the soldiers who carry out their assignments in a consistent manner. "In order to prevent such negative consequences and to fully carry out the order issued by the chief of the HVO main headquarters", then a number is given, of that order, "of 22nd April 1993, I hereby order ...", and then I will call your attention to paragraph 3: "Arrest immediately individuals or groups that get out of line and submit a warrant of arrest to the military police unit commander. "(4) you are responsible ..." -- Who would "you" be, Major? Would that be a reference to commanders of units within the zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "You are responsible for stopping the most extreme individuals and groups who have got out of line, do not protect civilians, burn and destroy civilian facilities", that is a reference to the groups who are doing those things, of course: "This conduct is sheer terrorism. Use all means available, including force, to prevent it." By reference to force, would that include force of arms, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, I am skipping the last two paragraphs for speed: "Commander Tihomir Blaskic, signed and stamped." If the recitation and the preamble are correct, Major, would you agree that that is indicative of an army that is not functioning properly, in which command and control has broken down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will not say broken down, but in an order like this, you are telling what to do if it should do, but some part of it, it seems, had to be necessary to give an order like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There has to be some remaining element of control or at least there is an attempt to preserve it, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that will be Defence exhibit 44?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is exhibit D44.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to make absolutely sure, Major -- and I have a few more questions, but I do intend to finish today, I assure you -- I would like to make it absolutely clear what portions of the conflict on April 16th you personally observed. You said early in the morning you heard artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were stopped at a checkpoint near Vitez and in the course of driving to that checkpoint, you could see smoke rising from portions of Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go into Vitez on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything else of the conflict on the morning of the 16th, any other aspects of it than what I have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall that was the morning where we saw those bodies at the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw five or more individuals laying on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some soldiers off to the side of the road in, I believe, black uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fired at us when we tried to go to those bodies to investigate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that, on the morning of the 16th did you see any other portions of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day of the 16th you spent in Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Travnik and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you spent it in Vitez, I am talking about the daylight hours now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The daylight hours we went to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the entire daylight hours of the 16th you were neither in the Vitez area or the Ahmici area; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to Vitez in the evening perhaps around 9.30 pm; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it considerably after the dinner hour? I suppose that depends on when your dinner hour is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we came back before dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go when you first came back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To our house in Vitez and after that we went to the British battalion and asked them what had happened in that area, because we were a little afraid if our house in Vitez was still there when we came back because of all the shellings in that area before we left it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left to drive to try and return to the Zenica on the evening of the 16th, did you make any other observations about the conflict, the fighting that was going on, or were you not in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you know, we had problems with our vehicle, and we wanted to go back to Zenica as quick as possible, so we did not allow ourselves to do anything else but just trying to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were tending to other business, so it is accurate, is it not, that until you started to drive home to Zenica from the point you arrived back in Vitez, you did not make any additional observations concerning the conflict that was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, but we heard at UNPROFOR, at the British battalion -- because normally when we had been out on a mission in Vitez, normally we went back and we had a visit with the British battalion, telling them about our findings as well, and then the British battalion told us about their findings. This was necessary because sometimes we were travelling in areas where the British battalion had not been and maybe we saw some HVO or BiH positions in those areas, so we just handed over our information to the British battalion and opposite. This was necessary for both of us because we were shot at several times from HVO positions and BiH positions, so therefore we have to help each other, so we were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You briefed them and they briefed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right now I am focusing on your personal observations, first hand observations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the evening then of the 16th, you left the BritBat base in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When driving east on the main Vitez/Busovaca road, you observed some tracer fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For about half an hour, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you came to a checkpoint at the Ahmici main road junction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from that vantage point you could see many houses burning in Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not able to go up into Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you went on to Zenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even if we could go in there, I do not think we had been able to do that because of what was happening there; we were not secure enough ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you were though you could not observe any fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only all the burning houses and then we saw a few persons in the road and in the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than what I have just described, did you see any other portions of the conflict itself on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us then from your own observations how many of the 250 to 300 men that you believe would be necessary for the infantry portion of the operation on 16th April, how many would have been required in Ahmici, or are you not able to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not able to say that. As I told you before, I have no experience in how to burn down villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your own eyes, you do not know very much, if anything, about the actual conflict in Ahmici, other than it ended with many, many homes being burned and obviously people being killed; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we know that all those burned houses were not the result of an artillery attack or a mortar attack, because if there have been used artillery or mortars against those buildings, it will normally not put on a fire of this size, so we discussed and we concluded that this fire was put on by -- some men have put on the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people would it take to burn down a village of that size? That would be the only empirical basis you would have to estimate manpower need; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many men were used in that and I have told you that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate your patience. I am trying to make sure the record is clear. You said that in your experience, there would be an HVO forward command post for an operation of the type undertaken on 16th April 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a normal procedure when an army is going to an operation, then the commander will command his unit from a forward headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the commander was not at the forward base, would that degrade in any way the ability of the commander to monitor and direct the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the commander is not present at the forward headquarters, a representative of the commander should be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or else it degrades the commander's ability to monitor and direct the operation; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends which order the commander gave to the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some time on April 16th, a phone call was placed to HVO headquarters at the hotel Vitez to try and reach Colonel Blaskic; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who placed that call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall that in the morning, we had a call from our headquarters in Zenica, they have been contacted by Hadzihasanovic asking ECMM to get in contact with Colonel Blaskic and ask for a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who placed the call to HVO headquarters? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was done by a Canadian lieutenant-colonel, Remi Landry, through our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you learned that Blaskic was away from the headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you infer from that that perhaps he was at a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because when all these were happening and we were not able to get in contact with Colonel Blaskic at his headquarters, then he was supposed to be at the forward headquarters. That is the normal way for a commander to react.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to search your memory. Did Remi Landry tell you that he was told that Blaskic was not at the headquarters or simply that he was not available? Do you remember, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, but we were not able to contact him at his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have a page of Mr. Remi Landry's statement placed in front of the witness, your Honour. I would like to see if it refreshes the witness's recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could place this one page before the witness? I would ask his assistance in placing it on the ELMO and that of the usher. Let me call your attention to the top line of the first full paragraph. It reads: "On the early morning of 16th April 1993", so that should help date the reference. Then the paragraph I am going to call your attention to is the third full paragraph beginning "This day ..." Why do we not put it on the ELMO, if you do not mind, and we can read it so everyone can understand the contents? If you could move the document up slightly, Major? Perfect, thank you. The paragraph I would like to call your attention to reads as follows: "This day, I also tried to get in touch with Colonel Blaskic, but I was informed by the HVO headquarters in Vitez that Colonel Blaskic was not available. I cannot recollect to whom I spoke. I was not told where Colonel Blaskic was, nor where I could get in touch with him. I cannot recollect what time I tried to get in touch with Colonel Blaskic this day." Does that refresh your memory, Major, with respect to what you were told on that day by Remi Landry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, we tried to contact him but we were not able to get in contact with him, but if it was because he was not available or he was not at his headquarters, I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you. You said in your direct testimony that you believed in the time-period of your tour that the army of BiH was a beaten army; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Lasva valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again if I could ask the usher's assistance? While that is occurring, your Honour, I believe the last page, just for the record, it will be Defence exhibit D45. The prior order of 24th April 1993 at 0920 hours would be D44. This excerpt of a document will be D46. Also for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have comments regarding D44, 45 and 46?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Only, Mr. President, in respect of Defence exhibit 45. Last week, I think you made it clear to both parties that if statements were going to be exhibited in evidence that the entire statement, in its totality, should be exhibited and not just extracts that are particularly relevant or material to one party, so we would ask that the entire statement be exhibited in evidence and not just one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do not need any of that exhibit admitted if the Prosecution objects. Our position is that anything can be used to attempt to refresh a witness whose memory needs refreshing. If one paragraph out of such a document is used, the Prosecution is free to use any other part of that document to seek to refresh recollection, but it does not make a 100-page book necessarily something that must be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are two questions. There is the question of principle and the number of pages. We have dealt with the question of principle upon your request, Mr. Hayman and Mr. Nobilo. Can you tell me how long is this report, this document? How long is it? Yes, you gave me the answer. In that case, the whole document will be admitted, regardless of the number of pages. D45 and then exhibit D46, please do not forget to give us the source of that document to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I was doing that, your Honour. This document was provided by the Prosecution and it has simply been identified -- let me consult with my counsel across the bar for a moment, your Honour, to check whether I may use a certain phrase. If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It has been identified to us, your Honour, as a Mil Info Summ, which I believe stands for military information summary generated by the Prince of Wales's own unit or company, dated 8th June 1993. Are you familiar, Major, with the Mil Info Summs generated by the UNPROFOR BritBat forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place this redacted portion of this Mil Info Summ on the ELMO? If you could move it over just a little? I apologise for having to ask you to assist us in this way. This portion, the pertinent portion of this Mil Info Summ I would like to call to your attention is as follows: "Bila valley. 2 Gen. The expected BiH offensive in the area has begun. A major Muslim push has been made down the Bila valley towards Vitez and Travnik. The villages of Guca Gora", and I will omit the grid or map indicators, "Brahovici, Grahovcici, Bukovica, Radonice and Maline have been captured by the BiH. C/S" -- do you know what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is call signs. That is the normal phrase they use for their units, patrols. Each patrol has their own call sign to use on the radio equipment. Normally the British Battalion were using C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It refers to one of the units out in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "C/S have witnessed atrocities being committed by the BiH in Guca Gora and C/SS are remaining there in order to provide local protection for the approximate 200 X Croat civilians who are surrounded by the attacking BiH troops. There is a mass move of Croats down through the Bila valley into the Vitez, Novi Bila and Busovaca areas." Major, this was on 8th June 1993. In fact, was the HVO driven out of Travnik within a short period of after this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall if it was out of Travnik, but I can recall that BiH did this, that was normally when even as I concluded it was a beaten army, a beaten army is not the same as an army who is not able to fight. Sometimes it was the only way they were able to survive was to make a counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall that during this attack, that HVO were shaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were shaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they starting to become the beaten army by this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the beaten army but I think that BiH succeeded in some of their attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention forward about a month in your tour to this document, which is also a Mil Info Summ from the Prince of Wales's own unit, dated 10th July 1993, that is Mil Info Summ, Prince of Wales' own or PWO, 10th July 1993, and I would like to read you the highlighted sections on your copy, if you would be so kind to put it on the ELMO again so that others can follow. Again this document, your Honour, provided to the Defence, I believe pursuant to our discovery motion. Paragraph 10, under the heading "Vitez": "A meeting with the CO" -- is that commonly a term representing commanding officer, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "A meeting with the commanding officer and Mimad Alagic, Commander Bosanska Krajina, revealed that Alagic is in command of approximately 12,000 BiH troops and that his current mission is to capture the remaining Croat enclaves of Vitez and Busovaca." Skipping down to heading A: "The aim of the current fighting is to capture the ammo factory", and there is a parenthetical reference to grid coordinates. After the end of the comment, the bottom of that paragraph, it continues: "The secondary objective in this specific area is to cut the HVO MSR." Do you know what MSR is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for a moment, but maybe a little later I will recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree it appears to refer to a territory or geographic area under the control of the HVO, something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well: "The secondary objective in this specific area is to cut the HVO MSR which connects Novi Bila with Vitez", again grid references. "B. More co-ordinated attacks will be made to cut the HVO MSR in the following areas: (i) Novi Bila; (ii) at the Dubravica T-junction; (iii) Nadioci; (iv) the Busovaca T-junction." Then skipping down to the comment that appears approximately eight lines from the bottom: "Comment. If successful, this operation will effectively isolate the Vitez area into five small pockets." Would you agree that the HVO in Vitez and Busovaca had far fewer than the 12,000 men referenced in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I do not think that this commander of this Bosanska Krajina had all those men. Sometimes commanders were telling you they had a lot of men, we do not always believe them. Here he states that he has all those men. If that is true, then there were more BiH soldiers in this operation than HVO soldiers, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not sure, did you answer my earlier question whether Travnik fell? Did the HVO lose Travnik in the June/July time-period of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered you that I cannot recall if Travnik fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO brigades had been expelled from Zenica back in April; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think actually MSR means "main supply routes".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which would connote some territorial connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the roads where they normally were using to bring in and out troops and ammunition and fuel and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time you departed the theatre, had the HVO also lost about half of its territory that it had held in the Novi Travnik municipality, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to request that these latest exhibits be admitted. I believe this most recent one will be D47.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is D47.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think that will mean that the only exhibit that I have tendered during this examination not admitted or not fully admitted will be the tape, D38. If I can confirm that? If there is no objection to the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The two videotapes for which the source has not been identified by my learned friend and secondly, the statement D45, which the court has requested be admitted in totality and not just one page as it is now, so those are the only two exhibits that we would object to being admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Regarding 45, that is not an objection, as we have ruled that the report be admitted in totality. As for the three tapes, for the first, we were told the source, local TV, as far as I recall. As for the two other clips, they have not been identified. Mr. Hayman could not give us the source. So should they be rejected or not? I am going to consult my colleagues (Pause). The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that these two clips should be admitted as evidence for two reasons: first that the witness recognised through the pictures the people. He did not, of course, identify the source, but he recognised the clips; and secondly, the judges are quite free, it is up to their discretion, to appreciate these two clips, knowing that the source was not formally identified. Therefore, Mme Fauveau, will you give us the numbers for these two tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually it is one tape with three clips. The first segment is D38A, the second D38B and D38C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my testimony. Thank you Major for sharing your testimony with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I turn to the Prosecution. Do you have any additional questions as this is your witness, Mr. Prosecutor, before my colleagues or I myself have some questions? It is 5.00 pm. Do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, a number of material issues have been raised by the Defence. I do have quite an extensive re-examination of this witness. I will make it as brief as I can. The witness is prepared to stay another day so that you and your brother judges may ask him further questions, but there are a number of matters which I feel I need to cover for the sake of completeness of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case you are going to begin straight away, of course on condition you are not going to do the examination-in-chief all over, only as regards what was new in the cross-examination. Remember that the judges are very attentive and I am sure you will bear that in mind. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor. Re-examined by MR. CAYLEY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President, thank you. Major Baggesen, in order to be as brief as I can I will try and address your cross-examination in blocks rather than go through each and every individual part of your testimony again. You remember that you testified both in your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination that certain civilian prisoners were released in Kiseljak on 21st June 1993; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those individuals that were released civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all dressed in civilian clothes and when we asked them whether they were civilians or soldiers they told us that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the HVO representative that was with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Mr. Pero Skopljak from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that these particular prisoners had actually come from digging trenches and clearing minefields. Did you complain to Mr. Skopljak about this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did Mr. Skopljak report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was supposed to respond to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your entire service in Central Bosnia, did you ever come across any soldiers who were prisoners of war in HVO prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in HVO prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity were those individuals in HVO prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all civilians, and we knew that because normally when we visit those, we have the opportunity to speak with them and they are all able to tell the same story, that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to your cross-examination about the HVO, my learned friend asked you certain questions about the level of health of HVO soldiers. Did you ever personally witness any ill-fed HVO soldiers in the Central Bosnian region that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, as I did not see any BiH soldiers who were starving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed I think at the Easter celebration that you attended in Vitez, how would you describe the quantity of food that was available there for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was good enough; it was a nice party with a lot of local dishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never witnessed any starving or hungry HVO soldiers in your three months in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now very briefly return to 16th April? You were in Vitez and later in Ahmici. On that day, did you see any Bosnian government soldiers in the area of Vitez or Ahmici, any at all? Did you see any individual soldiers or organised units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the only soldiers that you saw on that day in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can address your mind to the kidnapping of the five HVO officers, one of whom was kidnapped on 15th April, the other four considerably earlier, and we will not repeat that testimony, but the video clips that were shown by the Defence and which you identified are a ghastly sight. Was that a regular image that was seen on the television in Zenica and Vitez? Was it unusual that such an image should be seen on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because there was a local TV station in Zenica and there was TV Vitez, and those were the two medias who were doing their best to inform the public of what had happened and incidents, so it was just to see the news that every day or every second day we were able to see things -- not like the kidnapping, but we were able to see pictures of killed people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a regular occurrence to see such gory images on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it was a part -- normally the media was used for propaganda means. Of course, something like this fits in that, but normally we saw a lot of things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed the incident of the kidnapping of Commander Totic actually happened in a Bosnian government-controlled area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Bosnian government authorities in Zenica did not prevent the filming of these dead bodyguards and the bystander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And even the brigade commander attended a party hosted by the Bosnian Corps the night before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the brigade commander, you are referring to Commander Totic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, do you think that the kidnapping of the four staff officers in the Novi Travnik and Travnik area and the kidnapping of Zivko Totic had anything at all to do with what happened on 16th April in Vitez and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this incident with the kidnapped persons was an isolated incident, and the only reason for this incident was that the Mujahedins wanted to have something they were able to bargain with the HVO about, because at that time, HVO had already taken a lot of the Mujahedins in their custody and now the Mujahedins wanted to take some HVO in their custody so they were able to bargain. That is the normal way the Mujahedins are operating. You can see kidnappings like this in the Middle East and Lebanon and in Afghanistan. I think this incident had nothing to do with the rest of the conflict down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically the conflict that erupted on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not believe the kidnapping was related to the eruption of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your cross-examination, you were asked many questions on military structures and asked to compare Western European army headquarters structures to the HVO headquarters structure. You equated Colonel Blaskic's command in Vitez to a corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Danish Army, how large is an army corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 40 or 50,000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the HVO headquarters or the number of troops that Colonel Blaskic commanded considerably less than this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. I only called Colonel Blaskic's headquarters a corps level because the unit he commanded had the same size as Hadzihasanovic and he was a corps level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were many less troops than in a Western European corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were many less troops, you would expect there would be less staff officers in headquarters to command that much smaller corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Zenica shelling: from your memory, what was the distance of the nearest military target to where those six shells fell? Which shell fell closest to a military target and how far was it away from that target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember one of the impact was not -- the impact that was not at the marketplace or the bus stop -- I think there was two in the centre where one of the impacts were more in a western direction and I think from that impact to the nearest military -- not a headquarters but an office was 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not sure whether any of those offices were actually military targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my point of view, they were not military targets, because it was only a minor unit there. The only military target in that area was the corps headquarters at the steel factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of these offices that were 500 metres away when you are firing a weapon like this, what is the margin of error when you are firing from approximately 15 kilometres with a 122 millimetre howitzer in, let us say, a sideways direction to make it simple. What is the margin of error on a well-trained gun crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a well trained gun crew I would think 50 metres, but with a bad trained crew I think maybe 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was 5 times as bad as a badly trained gun crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not five times, from 50 to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said 100 metres would be a badly trained gun crew and this was 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your professional opinion, what was the target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that area where the impact was, and if you are looking those 100 metres to each side, I was not able to tell you that there were any military targets, so I think that this attack was carried out against a civilian target, and I think the aim of this attack was just to show that HVO were able to attack Zenica with artillery. I cannot see any approach but that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the casualties that were caused by that shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many but I think it was about 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but we heard that a lot of people have been killed at the marketplace, because there was normally a lot of people, civilians, sitting at the marketplace with a small desk selling cigarettes, changing money, because the local money down there because not -- you could not use the local money and you could -- I can remember one time I went to one of them with my zippo lighter and needed gas for my zippo lighter, small desks like that, so there were lots of people like that were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was well known there would have been lots of civilians in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could now move ahead, Major Baggesen, to your time on the Busovaca Joint Commission? Again I am going to move as quickly as I can. How long did you sit on this body approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, did you make regular complaint to the HVO representative about the conduct of HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the subject matter of those complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally we did the complaints after we came back to the ECMM house in the afternoon, where we discussed the fact-finding missions we had been on on these mixed teams, and then we made the complaints to HVO and to BiH about our findings and those complaints were normally on killing of civilian persons, burnt down houses, robbed houses and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the Busovaca Joint Commission established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it function for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think five months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge and from speaking to your colleagues, were complaints of the nature that you have just described made throughout that period to the HVO representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that HVO representative reporting to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franjo Nakic was normally reporting to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact I think the Defence said Mr. Nakic had been hand-picked for the job by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a man we trusted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Communications and orders, very briefly. In military operations, is it normal for a geographical area of command to be cut off from a commander? He may command in a particular area, but he may command another area that is cut off. Is that normal in wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Danish Army, is that any excuse for not properly organising your command, issuing orders, ensuring control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would not be able to ring up your General and say, "I am terribly sorry, General, I cannot make it to this particular area; we are cut off", no? I would just like to show you these orders again. If the witness could be shown Defence exhibit 39. In fact, while you are up, 39, 42A, 43A, 44A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have some of those up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place D39 on the ELMO? Major Baggesen, what is the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the order addressed to? If you could read it out to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is addressed to all commanders of units in Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and to brigades and independent units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could read the next line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Based on the request by the Chief of the HVO main headquarters", then a number --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can stop there. If you then go to the bottom of the document, and if you could read out to the court to whom copies of this order --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "A copy to files and a copy to ONO (operations and training body)."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the phrase "operations and training body" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is normally the staff officer and his men who are responsible for doing the operation and the training of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that Colonel Blaskic was actually addressing a copy of this order to that body, what would that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he had this body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he had an operations and training body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he had an establishment for the operations and for the training of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now move to the next document, D42A, which is the order of 17th March 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one dated 17th March?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. I would just like to refer you to where it says "for the attention of" and if you could read to whom this order was addressed by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not object to questions about the document, but the document speaks for itself, so to have him read portions I think unnecessarily takes up time and is beneath the expertise of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could comment? It is actually material to the Prosecutor's case to whom Colonel Blaskic was addressing his orders. Mr. Hayman omitted to read part of the document; it is only fair to both parties that a complete picture is presented to the court, and not only part of it which is actually beneficial to one particular party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They should be admitted in their entirety, translated in their entirety, as part of the record, but what I am saying is to have a witness simply read a portion -- I am going to want to read other portions. It does not end anywhere. These documents will speak for themselves. If he has a question about meaning or something like that, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I should like to remind you that this document was submitted to the Trial Chamber by you as evidence.
